run.question: The payment-api pod in namespace app-259 had issues on November 20, 2026 around 13:45 UTC. What happened?

report.summary: Log evidence from Loki shows that the payment-api pod payment-api-259-d8f7b9c4-abc12 in namespace app-259 (job/service label payment-api) began logging 'Failed to acquire database connection - pool exhausted' at 13:46:00 UTC on 2026-11-20 and logged 8 such ERROR lines through 14:44:00 UTC, all with multi-second connection-acquisition waits (wait_time_ms 1227-4840) and queue lengths of 5-15. Across the whole authorized window (2026-11-20T06:41:39Z to 2026-11-21T06:41:39Z) these 8 lines are the only ERROR lines; before 13:46 only INFO 'Payment processed successfully' lines appear (11:19, 11:40, 11:44, 12:57, 13:42), and after 14:44 only successful-payment INFO lines appear up to 05:32 on 2026-11-21. So the pod was not down: payments still succeeded at 13:59 and 14:49 while some requests failed to get a DB connection. A log keyword search for startup/listening/WARN/timeout/retry/pool/connection strings in 13:00-15:30 returned only those 8 pool-exhaustion lines, which is counter-evidence to a restart or a different error class in the logs. The trigger beyond the pod is unresolved: Kubernetes, Prometheus and Jaeger were unavailable during this run, no database service logs exist in Loki, and only one payment-api pod series was observed. Thus the pod's own DB-connection-pool exhaustion is a fact, while whether a saturated/slow payment database underlies it remains an unverified hypothesis.

claims.text: Pod payment-api-259-d8f7b9c4-abc12 in namespace app-259 (labels job=payment-api, service=payment-api) logged ERROR 'Failed to acquire database connection - pool exhausted' at 13:46, 13:54, 14:03, 14:15, 14:19, 14:21, 14:31 and 14:44 UTC on 2026-11-20; a query of {namespace="app-259", level="ERROR"} over the full authorized window with limit 500 returned exactly these 8 lines, the earliest at 13:46:00Z and the latest at 14:44:00Z.

The pool-exhaustion lines carry growing connection-acquisition waits and queues: wait_time_ms 1227 (13:46, queue_length 10), 2104 (13:54, 11), 1495 (14:03, 8), 2965 (14:15, 9), 4005 (14:19, 10), 4840 (14:21, 8), 2358 (14:31, 15), 3836 (14:44, 5).

Before the incident the same pod logged only INFO 'Payment processed successfully' lines - PAY-2676 at 11:19, PAY-7644 at 11:40, PAY-5973 at 11:44, PAY-1813 at 12:57 and PAY-5032 at 13:42 on 2026-11-20 - with no ERROR lines in the 06:41:39Z-13:45:00Z portion of the authorized window.

The pod kept serving some payments during and after the error burst: INFO 'Payment processed successfully' at 13:59 (PAY-1800), 14:49, 15:27, 17:01, 17:38, 19:25, 20:09, 21:47, 21:52, 22:19, 00:30, 00:34, 01:12, 01:39, 03:15, 03:54 and 05:32 on 2026-11-21, with no ERROR lines returned after 14:44.

A keyword-filtered query over {namespace="app-259"} for 'WARN|warn|timeout|slow|retry|pool|connection|started|listening|Starting' in 13:00-15:30Z returned only the 8 'pool exhausted' ERROR lines (limit 200 not reached, so no matching startup, listening, WARN, timeout or retry lines were returned for that window).

Only one payment-api pod series was observed in Loki in 13:00-15:00Z: sum by (pod_name, job, namespace) of count_over_time returned a single series {namespace="app-259", job="payment-api", pod_name="payment-api-259-d8f7b9c4-abc12"}, and sum by (namespace, job) over 13:40-14:00Z returned a single series job=payment-api, namespace=app-259.

Logs of the database dependency are not present in the Loki source examined: a cluster-wide line query {namespace=~".+"} over the authorized window returned 20 lines / 2 streams, all labelled job=payment-api, namespace=app-259, service=payment-api (that query hit its 20-line limit, so its coverage of other workloads is incomplete).

Per-level log counts over 30-minute windows show the ERROR series appearing from the evaluation point covering 13:46 while INFO lines continue at a low background rate throughout 13:00-15:00, i.e. the error condition started at 13:46 rather than being present earlier in that period.

The pod was not fully down or crash-looping from the log perspective: it emitted ERROR lines and successful-payment INFO lines in the same period (e.g. PAY-1800 at 13:59 between errors at 13:54 and 14:03), so this is partial failure of payment processing, not a total outage of the pod.

Pod restart / container startup problem as the explanation of the 13:45 incident is not supported by the logs: no startup, 'listening' or similar boot lines were returned in 13:00-15:30Z for the pod, and successful-payment lines continue across the window; the pod name stayed payment-api-259-d8f7b9c4-abc12 throughout. Kubernetes pod status, restart counts and events could not be read to confirm this independently.

The exhaustion may be caused by the payment database (or the connection path to it) being slow or saturated rather than by payment-api itself: acquisition waits of 1.2-4.8 s with queues of 5-15 connections are consistent with connections not being returned/served fast enough by the dependency. This is not verified - no database logs, DB metrics or traces were obtainable in this run.

Alternatively the pod's own connection-pool sizing / leak (max pool size, idle or timeout settings applied to payment-api) may be too small for its concurrency, which would also present as 'pool exhausted' with growing queue_length; verifying this requires the payment-api ConfigMap/Secret and pool metrics, which were not readable.

A possible load-driven trigger is plausible because the error burst (13:46-14:44) coincides with extra log volume in the pod's stream (count_over_time rose from 1 to 2-3 lines per 10 minutes around 13:46-14:44), but log volume in this sampled source cannot quantify request load and no traffic metric was available, so this remains unverified.

gaps: Kubernetes API was unavailable in this run (kubernetes_jq_query, kubernetes_tabular_query and kubernetes_count all returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE), so pod status, container restart counts, last termination reason/exit code, owner chain (ReplicaSet/Deployment) and pod events for payment-api-259-d8f7b9c4-abc12 could not be read.

Prometheus was unavailable in this run (get_metric_names, get_label_values, execute_prometheus_instant_query, metrics_range_query and get_prometheus_target all returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE), so no error-rate, rpc latency or kube-state-metrics series were obtained; a DB-related or pool-related metric series would be unknown rather than zero.

Jaeger was unavailable in this run (traces_list_services and traces_search returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE), so no span-level status or duration evidence exists and caller/downstream impact of the failed payment requests is unverified.

No logs from the payment database or any other dependency exist in the accessible Loki data (only job=payment-api, namespace=app-259 streams were returned), so the database instance, its health and the trigger of the pool exhaustion remain unidentified.
The Loki log set is sparse (e.g. only 8 lines in the pod's 13:00-14:30 window), so observed error counts are a lower bound and the exact error rate is unknown.
ConfigMaps/Secrets holding DB pool settings could not be read (secrets are not readable), so pool size/timeout configuration and any fault-injection settings were not verified.
Whether end users or upstream callers saw failures is not observed; no metric or trace evidence covers them.
next_steps: When Kubernetes access is restored, read the pod's status, restart count, last termination state and events, and follow the owner chain (Deployment -> ReplicaSet -> Pod) for payment-api-259-d8f7b9c4-abc12 to confirm the pod was not restarted and check for OOMKilled or Evicted conditions.
Inspect the payment-api ConfigMap (DB pool max size, connection/idle timeouts) and compare it with the observed queue lengths up to 15 and waits up to 4.8 s.
Check the payment database's own metrics/logs (connections in use, max_connections, latency) over 13:30-15:00 UTC on 2026-11-20 to test the dependency-saturation hypothesis.

Re-run the Prometheus queries for payment/DB error-rate and latency series and Jaeger searches for error spans once those backends are reachable, to determine which callers were affected and whether latency deviated from a pre-incident baseline.
